assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, bring thousands of atoms to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18. They are the clearest case on this list of precision atomic physics opening new fundamental tests, such as gravitational redshift over millimetres, searches for variation of constants and a possible redefinition of the second. The work is original, conceptually clean and very well understood.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice and made the first demonstrations. Ye's JILA group drove the systematic accuracy, Sr clock comparisons and the many-body clock work. The two-person configuration is natural. Others, such as Hall and Hansch (frequency combs, 2005) and Wineland (ion clocks, 2012), are already recognised and are not credited here. Some of the Sr-lattice priority history between groups is not fully known to me.
assessment.maturity: Many independent laboratories (RIKEN/Tokyo, JILA, NIST, PTB, SYRTE, NPL) reproduce and compare these clocks. The interpretation is stable, and the field is ready for recognition now.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would give weight to the pending redefinition of the second, which has not yet happened.
Relative credit for early lattice-clock demonstrations among several groups is not fully clear to me from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The recollision picture (the three-step model) and its quantum version (the strong-field approximation for high-harmonic generation and above-threshold ionization) explain the plateau that was once such a surprise. They are the conceptual basis of attosecond science, and they also give laser-driven electron diffraction and orbital imaging. The picture is simple and original and gives deep understanding, which I value highly.
assessment.attribution: Corkum's 1993 recollision model and the Lewenstein-L'Huillier-Salieres-Corkum 1994 quantum theory are the decisive contributions. Corkum is clearly central. Lewenstein's theory role is strong, but the 1994 paper has several authors, notably L'Huillier, who is already a laureate (2023). A fair two-person split here is reasonable but could be contested, and I note that I know L'Huillier and the Lund group well, so I should be careful with my own judgement on this entry.
assessment.maturity: Fully verified by many experiments and used widely in attosecond metrology. The 2023 prize recognised the experimental pulses but did not explicitly recognise the underlying theory, so a prize on the theory is timely and does not repeat the earlier award.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as already covered by the 2023 prize.
The proper balance among the several authors of the 1994 quantum theory.
My personal proximity to the Lund and Lewenstein-adjacent community.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, with the superfluid-to-Mott transition, Fermi-Hubbard antiferromagnetism and single-site quantum gas microscopy. They give controlled access to quantum many-body questions that solid-state materials cannot answer. This is a wide and mature programme with real fundamental reach.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation. Greiner and Bloch did the Mott-insulator experiment, and Bloch also led the microscope and many-body programme. Esslinger (Fermi Mott insulator), Cirac, Hansch and others are credited by the list but I leave them out. A three-person split is sensible but leaves obvious omissions, and the theory-versus-experiment balance is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Mature, and reproduced by many groups worldwide. Quantum simulation is still developing, so its ultimate scientific yield (for example on the Fermi-Hubbard phase diagram) is not fully known.
uncertainties: Many deserving contributors (Esslinger, Cirac, Hansch, Ketterle-type BEC lineage) cannot all be included.
Whether the main impact is a conceptual breakthrough or an enabling technology.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cirac and Zoller's proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and, with others, for atomic quantum simulation turned a vague idea into a concrete experimental programme. It underlies ion-trap quantum computers and much of AMO quantum information. The scientific originality is high.
assessment.attribution: Both names are credited as a pair and are plainly the decisive theorists for the 1995 trapped-ion gate proposal. The pair also overlaps with B016, so a prize on one entry would complicate the other. Experimental implementers (Wineland's group, Blatt, Monroe) are not credited here and the 2012 prize already honoured ion control.
assessment.maturity: The ion-trap platform is confirmed by many laboratories, and quantum computing demonstrations are advancing. The theory is mature. The question is whether quantum computing itself is yet mature enough for a prize.
uncertainties: Overlap with the optical-lattice entry, since Zoller appears in both.
The relation to the 2012 and 2022 quantum-information-related prizes, which might lower the priority.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics reaches the quantum ground state of mechanical oscillators, with sideband cooling, optomechanically induced transparency, squeezing and entanglement of macroscopic objects. It speaks directly to my favourite question: where does the quantum world end and the everyday world begin? The conceptual interest is high.
assessment.attribution: Aspelmeyer, Kippenberg and Painter led the key experiments in the quantum regime (ground-state cooling, strong coupling, quantum control). Earlier cooling work by Kippenberg and by others, and the theoretical groundwork by Girvin, Marquardt, Clerk and others, are also relevant. A three-person list is plausible but not obviously settled.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed by several independent groups. The applications are still developing and the field has not yet produced a single definitive landmark result, so recognition may be a bit early.
uncertainties: Credit among many groups, including theorists not listed.
Whether the field has a single clear discovery rather than a broad programme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube detected a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos at TeV-PeV energies and later identified TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane as sources. This opened neutrino astronomy and is a clear discovery of something previously unseen. I defer to colleagues in astroparticle physics on the detailed assessment.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led IceCube, Karle contributed key detector and instrument leadership, and Spiering is credited for the earlier pioneering DUMAND/Baikal-era efforts. Collaboration-scale discoveries make a three-name allocation difficult, and the role of other leaders (e.g. Baikal and AMANDA contributors) is not clear to me.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is robustly confirmed, with independent support from ANTARES-type and KM3NeT-type work, but source identification is still developing. Recognition would be timely but some interpretations are not yet stable.
uncertainties: Source identification beyond TXS 0506+056 is still being established.
Credit allocation in a large collaboration with many leaders.
I have limited expertise in astroparticle physics.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry makes matter-wave sensors of extraordinary precision, used for measuring gravity, the fine-structure constant and for tests of the equivalence principle. This is core AMO physics with a direct fundamental flavour and clear applications in inertial sensing.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometry), Pritchard (the first atom interferometers with gratings) and Kasevich (with Chu, light-pulse interferometry) are central. Chu's own work is already honoured in 1997, and Muller and others contributed more recently. Allocation is difficult because the early 1991 experiments came from several groups at about the same time.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced, and the sensitivity is rising steadily. The headline fundamental-physics results (e.g. equivalence-principle tests and gravitational-wave proposals) have not yet reached the highest level, so it is arguably on the borderline of maturity.
uncertainties: Overlap with the earlier laser-cooling prizes of 1997.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Squeezed light reduces quantum noise below the shot-noise limit and is now used in gravitational-wave detectors, improving their reach in an operating observatory. It combines a deep quantum-optics idea with a clear practical test.
assessment.attribution: Caves proposed squeezed-light interferometry, Kimble produced early squeezed light, and Schnabel developed the frequency-dependent squeezing in GEO600 and later detectors. Mavalvala and the LIGO teams made important contributions that I leave out. Squeezing also has earlier foundations (Yuen, Slusher, Walls, others), which complicates a clean attribution.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed in LIGO, Virgo and GEO600, so the confirmation is strong. The conceptual novelty is partly older, and the 2017 prize for LIGO already covers much of the observational payoff.
uncertainties: Complex history with many early contributors.
The overlap with the 2017 LIGO recognition.
Whether this is better seen as an enabling method than a discovery.
